title: COP31 draft drops all mention of fossil fuels as Antalya climate talks head into overtime
dek: Thursday's slimmed-down text keeps a warning that warming may overshoot 1.5°C but removes Monday's call to phase out fossil fuels; the summit is due to end on Friday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, published a slimmed-down draft of the summit's main decision on Thursday that drops every reference to ending or limiting the use of fossil fuels, according to reports, a day before the talks are scheduled to close. The first draft, published on Monday, had called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels".

The new text keeps an acknowledgement that global warming could overshoot the 1.5°C limit set in the Paris Agreement, calls for "deep, rapid and sustained" cuts in greenhouse gas emissions and encourages scaling up technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the air, reports said. It is expected to be revised again before any deal, and delegates said the talks were likely to run past Friday's deadline, into Saturday.

## From the first draft to the second

The first draft of the "cover decision", an unedited 18-page text dated 16 November, had two consecutive paragraphs on fossil fuels. One urged countries to accelerate the "transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just, orderly and equitable manner" agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023; the next called for "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels". It also proposed that countries contribute, "in a nationally determined manner", to raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, and expressed "serious concern" at the spread of unilateral trade measures linked to climate, a point pressed by developing countries.

That draft drew objections from both sides. According to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin, the independent record of the talks, the Like-Minded Developing Countries, a bloc that includes India, said on Monday that it crossed their "red lines", including the 35 per cent electrification target and a roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels that singled out methane. The Arab Group and Russia rejected the text outright, opposing language that targets specific energy sources and "top-down" sectoral targets. The European Union's envoy said it needed "significant change", but from the other direction, wanting stronger language on cutting emissions.

It is not yet clear from reports whether the electrification target and the trade language survive in Thursday's version. The COP31 presidency, shared between Türkiye as host and Australia, which is steering the negotiations, has said the drafts are meant to narrow over the week and that the first text was "not intended to reflect consensus".

## The science behind the fight

The fossil-fuel language matters because burning coal, oil and gas is the main source of the carbon dioxide driving global warming. The first draft expressed "deep concern" at scientific findings on overshooting 1.5°C, noted that global efforts "remain insufficient to keep 1.5°C within reach", and proposed a work programme on the science of returning warming below 1.5°C by the end of the century. It also said carbon dioxide removal "will be required" to bring temperatures back down, but must complement, not replace, deep emission cuts.

A separate dispute concerns the timing of the next assessment report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's scientific review. European, African and Pacific countries want it ready before the next global stocktake in 2028; Saudi Arabia has said it is not seeking to delay climate science.

## India's position

Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav has said India will play a "bridge-building" role and has argued that "equitable access to the remaining, depleted, carbon budget is non-negotiable", according to reports. India opposes new top-down targets on developing countries, wants climate finance treated as an obligation of developed countries under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, and has backed a country-driven mechanism for a just transition. Removing the fossil-fuel language eases pressure on coal, which still generates most of India's electricity, but India has also said it wants stronger finance and technology commitments that the drafts have not yet delivered.

## What happens next

The summit is due to close on Friday, 20 November, but recent COPs have often run more than a day over. Further drafts are expected overnight. Any final decision needs consensus among nearly 200 countries, so a single bloc can still block the text.
